subject: US chip rule now reaches data centres in five countries
bodyMarkdown:
Washington spent three years deciding who was allowed to buy Nvidia's best chips. This week it started deciding where those chips are allowed to sit, and the rule went on the books while most of us were asleep.

## What the new rule actually does

CNBC reported on Wednesday that the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security has issued an **interim final rule**, meaning one that takes effect immediately while the public comment window stays open, requiring export licences for advanced AI chips headed to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The trigger is **total processing performance**, a single number that combines a chip's speed and its precision to measure how much compute it delivers. Quartz and NBC News reported that an overseas data centre supplying more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in China now needs a licence to get the hardware, and that facilities already serving those customers have 90 days to apply. There is a carve-out if the buyer is headquartered in the United States and the exporter reports the sale. The rule was filed on Monday and set for publication yesterday, with comments due inside 60 days.

## Why Washington bothered

The timing is not an accident. CNBC reported on Thursday that a House Foreign Affairs Committee review found the Commerce Department approved roughly 879,000 AI chip shipments to Chinese firms between December 2025 and May 2026, including about 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. Very few of those chips appear to have physically moved. Nvidia said on its third quarter earnings call that it has halted H200 shipments to China, and that H200 sales there came to less than 1 per cent of data centre revenue in the quarter ended in July. Reuters reported that several large Chinese internet companies each obtained around 10,000 of them. So the chips mostly stayed home, while the compute was rented offshore instead. That is the hole this rule is meant to close.

## Where Canada sits in this

Canada is not on the list of five, and I would not read that as a compliment. We are not a transshipment worry because we are not yet a serious exporter of compute. BCG published work this year putting Canada's AI data centre capacity at roughly 0.3 gigawatts today against 3.5 to 4 gigawatts of announced plans. Every one of those planned megawatts runs on American-designed chips bought under American licensing rules, which means Ottawa's sovereign compute ambitions depend on a licence regime it does not write and was not consulted on. The rule also shows how fast the perimeter can move. A control that covered buyers on Monday covered landlords by Thursday, and nothing in the text stops the next version from naming more countries.

## The takeaway

Watch two dates. The 90 day clock for existing data centres runs out around mid-February, which is when we find out whether BIS is actually processing licences or quietly denying them, and the 60 day comment window closes in late January, when Singapore, Malaysia and the hyperscalers will put their objections in writing. If you hold Nvidia through an index fund, watch what management says about China revenue at the next guidance update, since the company has already told you H200 sales there ran under 1 per cent of data centre revenue. And if you are following Canada's data centre buildout, ask who signs the export licence before you ask who owns the building.
